title: E-cigarette-related Nicotine Misinformation on Social Media
screen_reason: Content analysis of a random subsample of ENDS-related tweets; reports the share of tweets presenting nicotine/addiction information that contained potential misinformation, with an explicit denominator (41.7%, n=377 of 904). This is a CONTENT prevalence estimate against researcher coding anchored to peer-reviewed/agency evidence.

estimates.country: Not stated (Twitter keyword collection, no geographic filter; US-focused framing)
estimates.measure_type: % of ENDS-related tweets that presented nicotine/addiction information and contained at least one piece of potential misinformation
estimates.denominator: 904 tweets coded as presenting ENDS-related nicotine or addiction information, from a 2% simple random subsample (n=3,116) of 155,804 unique keyword-matched tweets
estimates.definition: Tweet coded as containing at least one of: anti-vaping exaggeration, pro-vaping exaggeration, nicotine is not addictive or is never harmful, or nicotine has unproven health benefits; codes were not mutually exclusive
estimates.misinfo_def: “Coders were instructed to determine the presence of potential misinformation based on the current literature from peer-reviewed scientific journals or reputable governmental or health agencies, such as the Centers for Disease Control & Prevention, at the time of the tweet.”
estimates.source_quote: Of tweets coded as presenting information, 41.7% (n=377) contained at least one piece of potential misinformation, meaning that they were coded as containing anti-vaping exaggeration, pro-vaping exaggeration, statements indicating that nicotine is not addictive or is never harmful, and/or statements indicating that nicotine has unproven health benefits.
estimates.page_loc: Results, ‘Presentation of information as fact’, p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two experienced graduate-level coders, iterative codebook development over 6 rounds with adjudication by the lead author; judged against peer-reviewed literature and reputable government/health agency guidance at the time of the tweet. Cohen's κ for tweet-content codes 0.72–1.00 (anti-vaping exaggeration 0.79, pro-vaping exaggeration 0.72, nicotine not addictive/never harmful 1.0, unproven health benefits 1.0, nicotine/addiction information 0.80); κ 0.85–1.00 for account type.
estimates.moderator_quote: Using open source “RITHM” software(Colditz et al., 2018), approximately 10.1 million tweets matching ENDS-related keywords (JUUL*, vape*, ecig*, e-cig*) were collected from April 2018 through March 2019. ... Tweets containing keywords related to nicotine or addiction (nicotine* and/or addict*) were then identified, which included 155,804 unique tweets and 578,561 retweets. ... A 2% subsample resulted in 3,116 unique tweets
estimates.notes: Denominator is tweets that PRESENTED information (904), not all relevant tweets (2,943) — the paper's headline framing. Year recorded as 2018 (collection window Apr 2018–Mar 2019). No geographic filter was applied to the keyword collection, so country coded Global despite the paper's US framing. Breadth = misleading because the numerator is dominated by exaggeration/distortion of otherwise true claims, not fabrication.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The four misinformation categories are reported separately against the same 904 denominator (anti-vaping exaggeration 21.6%, n=195; pro-vaping exaggeration 16.6%, n=150; nicotine not addictive or never harmful 2.5%, n=23; unproven health benefits 1.9%, n=17; Table 2). These are non-mutually-exclusive component types of the single headline estimate rather than stricter/broader definitions of misinformation, so per R4 only the headline 41.7% is kept as a row. (2) 'Of the users classified as bots, only 10 (9.3%) were coded as sharing misinformation' — a share of accounts (denominator 107 bot accounts) that posted misinformation. Not extracted: bots are a small non-headline subgroup (3.97% of 2,695 users) with no comparable human-user figure, and the denominator is a classifier-defined account class rather than a population of interest. (3) 94.5% of tweets coded as relevant to ENDS and 30.7% presenting information are relevance/topicality shares, not misinformation shares, so no rows. (4) Account-type breakdowns within each misinformation category (e.g. 78.5% of anti-vaping exaggeration tweets from individual accounts) describe who posted, not prevalence.

rob.design: Platform content analysis. Frame: 10.1M ENDS keyword tweets (JUUL*, vape*, ecig*, e-cig*) collected Apr 2018–Mar 2019 via RITHM; filtered to nicotine*/addict* keywords (155,804 unique tweets); 2% simple random subsample (n=3,116) human-coded. No response rate (platform data). Two experienced graduate-level coders, iterative 3-step codebook development, 6 rounds of double-coding 100 tweets with lead-author adjudication; Cohen's κ 0.72–1.00 for content codes and 0.85–1.00 for account type; remaining tweets coded independently (single-coded). Bot classification via Botometer at a 0.43 cutoff.
rob.item6_quote: Tweets coded as presenting information were then coded for the presence of misinformation in four categories: nicotine is not addictive or is never harmful, unproven health benefits, anti-vaping exaggeration, and pro-vaping exaggeration (Table 1). If the information in the tweet could not be disproven based on scientific literature, the tweet was coded as without clear misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Of the 3116 human-coded tweets, 2,943 (94.5%) were coded as relevant to ENDS. Of relevant tweets, 30.7% (n=904) presented ENDS-related nicotine or addiction information. Of tweets coded as presenting information, 41.7% (n=377) contained at least one piece of potential misinformation
